label: O(n**2)
evidence: The main two-pointer loops advance p and q monotonically for O(n) total, but ReverseSeq recurses on s[1..] and concatenates at every level, which is quadratic; the Python D[::-1] is O(n), so the agreement is accidental.

label: O(n)
evidence: Two sequential single passes over a_list (the sum and the prefix-sum scan) cost O(n) with n the length of c; the bounds x and y are only compared, never looped to.

label: O(1)
evidence: Straight-line code: one division, one modulus and a conditional increment, with no loop or recursion, so O(1) apart from IntToString which is charged 1.

evidence: The loop subtracts at most 5 from x per iteration, so it runs about number/5 times; the single integer input is the problem size n, which the label O(n) names directly.

evidence: One loop over the |grid| query rows, each doing constant work on row[0..3] and appending an O(1)-sized string; n counts queries and the integer values are only compared and printed.

label: O(logn)
evidence: The loop halves m each iteration until it reaches 1, so it runs about log2(n) times where n is the single integer input, which is the problem size the label names.

label: O(nlogn)
evidence: SortInts costs O(n log n) and every other loop (map build, whereIs, dp, resArr) is a linear pass with O(1) map and seq updates; JoinInts is linear, and the Python also sorts, so label and Dafny agree.

label: O(n)
evidence: One pass over a_list with O(1) map updates plus a single d.Keys materialisation and a loop over at most n distinct keys; ParseInt is charged per short numeric string, so the total is O(n).

label: O(n**2)
evidence: Nested loops both bounded by |a_list| compare every pair of elements, matching the Python numArray.count(x) inside a loop over numArray, which is quadratic.

label: O(n)
evidence: One loop to n with O(1) amortised appends to partA and partB, then JoinInts over the 2n-element concatenation, which is linear; the Python is also linear in n.

label: O(n)
evidence: The loop runs n times (n counting test cases) doing constant work on two-element rows, and Join over the n answer lines is linear in the output; the sizes 1..100 are only compared.

label: O(n**2)
evidence: For each of the |d_list| points the inner loop scans all distinct directions collected so far in dxs and dys, and has no early exit, so it is quadratic in the worst case, as is the Python scan over the set.

label: O(n+m)
what_to_look_for: The label O(n+m) assumes each element costs O(1). Find BitOr in the Dafny: it recurses with a/2 and b/2 until one argument is 0, so each call costs the bit length of the values. Then check the Python line f1|=int(x), a machine-word OR that is O(1) for values up to 10^9; if so the Python is O(n+m) and only the Dafny pays the value term.
evidence: BitOr is a hand-written recursion that halves both arguments, costing O(log max a_i) per call, so the Dafny is O(n log max a + m log max b); Python's | on ints of at most 10^9 is O(1), so the translation reimplemented a primitive and the Python really is O(n+m).

label: O(n**2)
what_to_look_for: The label O(n**2) counts only the (l, r) pairs. Find the two BitOr calls in the inner loop: BitOr recurses once per bit of its arguments, adding a log of the element values per iteration. Then compare the Python's s_a | ps[r], a constant-time machine OR for values at most 10^9; if so the Python is O(n**2) and only the Dafny pays the value term.
evidence: Each of the O(n**2) inner iterations calls BitOr twice and BitOr recurses on a/2 and b/2, costing O(log max a_i), so the Dafny is O(n**2 log max a); the Python | operator is O(1) at these magnitudes, so the translation introduced the extra factor.

label: O(nlogn)
what_to_look_for: The label assumes parsing is linear. Find ParseIntList in the Dafny: it builds the list with [ParseInt(ss[0])] + ParseIntList(ss[1..]), so every level concatenates onto a result of size n-i, which costs O(|t|) per level and is quadratic overall. Compare the Python list(map(int, input().split())), which is O(n); if the concat is charged as written, the row is O(n**2).
evidence: Solve calls ParseIntList(SplitWs(a_list_str)), whose prepend-concat [x] + ParseIntList(s[1..]) rebuilds the whole tail at each of n levels for O(n**2), while the sort and binary-search loop is O(n log n) and the Python parse is linear, so the Python matches the label and the Dafny does not.

label: O(n)
what_to_look_for: The label O(n) treats n (the number of test cases) as the size. Find Repeat("3", v - 1) in the loop over a_list and check the statement: each v is a per-test digit count up to 10^5 and Repeat is linear in v. If the output length is the real cost, the label omits it; it would only stand if every v were bounded by a literal.
evidence: Each iteration builds "2" + Repeat("3", v - 1), costing O(v) in the per-test value v, so the total is O(sum of the per-test v_i), not O(number of tests); the Python "3" * (v - 1) pays the same, so the label is wrong, not the translation.

label: O(n)
what_to_look_for: The label O(n) counts cells but each cell's processing depends on its own text. Find NumToLetters, which recurses on the numeric column value (depth log base 26), and ParseInt and DigitRunLen, which scan the cell's characters. The statement caps coordinates at 10^6, so each term is at most about 14 characters; decide whether that per-cell width counts as a constant or as a missing value or width parameter.
evidence: Per cell the Dafny pays O(len(cell)) in DigitRunLen, ParseInt and LettersToNum and O(log26 col) in NumToLetters, and the Python g and f lambdas pay the same, so the total is O(sum of cell lengths) rather than strictly O(n); the cap makes each term tiny, so I lean to O(n).

label: O(n)
evidence: Three sequential linear loops: initialising l of size N+1, one pass over a_list for the updates, and a min scan over l; N equals the length of the permutation and every seq update is O(1).
